issues.explanation: The threat items are oriented toward external environmental danger (scanning surroundings, planning escape routes), which is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 68-year-old policy analyst unless there is an additional trauma context not represented here.

Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance reinforces an expectation of unpredictable external danger, which fits assault/combat-type trauma more than illness trauma and does not cohere well with the rest of the illness-based profile.

Memory: Guilt on Recall and Negative Appraisals: Character Blame imply a strong self-blame/guilt formulation, but the other selected items center on current danger vigilance and emotional loss; for life-threatening illness, this specific self-blame pattern is possible but, combined with the external-danger threat items, creates a clinically incoherent mix of trauma themes.

For a life-threatening illness trauma, persistent escape-route scanning is hard to reconcile with the trauma context. It implies imminent external attack or entrapment rather than illness-related threat, while the rest of the profile centers on bodily danger and emotional change.

Intense guilt on recall is not impossible after severe illness, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile: the appraisals focus on permanent emotional loss and bodily alarm rather than responsibility for causing harm or failing others. The guilt theme lacks support elsewhere in memory or appraisals.

'The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am' suggests a strong characterological self-blame formulation. In a life-threatening illness case, that can occur, but in this profile it is not well integrated with the other selected appraisals, which focus on bodily danger and emotional numbing. Together with guilt on recall, it introduces a self-blame theme that is otherwise unsupported.

vignette: Malcolm Thorne was sixty-six when a sudden cascade of organ failure collapsed him into his own body, a life-threatening illness that turned his bedroom into a monitored space and his breathing into a constant vigil. For three weeks, he lay tethered to equipment, each beep and hiss a potential warning that his lungs or heart would simply stop. What frightened him most was not the pain, but the unpredictability of his physiology; every time his chest hitched, he braced for another crisis. By the time he was discharged, the acute danger had passed, but Malcolm had come to believe that the threat remained. He noticed his shoulders had drawn up, tight and unyielding, as if still ready to react to danger. Even inside his own home, where the doors were locked and the familiar objects waited on their shelves, he felt on guard, scanning the hallway for any unfamiliar sound. He managed the house alone since becoming widowed, and the quiet rooms, once a comfort, now felt like places where he had to remain watchful. As the weeks turned into months, his days as a policy analyst became a steady navigation of parallel experiences. Sitting at his drafting table, sorting through legislative briefs and funding allocations, he had difficulty concentrating. The words on the page remained clear while his attention drifted to the pulse in his wrist or the rhythm of his breathing. He was certain that his body kept reacting as if he were still in the hospital, treating minor stresses as emergencies. When a memory of the illness returned, it did so without the usual passage of time; the memory felt like it was happening right now rather than something that was over. Sometimes, however, he could recall what happened but felt completely numb, as if it had happened to a stranger. What frightened him most was the sudden shift between these two states: one moment he would be reading a policy draft, detached and distant, and the next the emotional weight would crash down, so overwhelming that he had to stop, set his pen down, and wait. These experiences solidified into quiet convictions. Malcolm had come to believe he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, that the illness had left his daily life in a permanent state of suspension. He could no longer trust his own body; a simple cough or a skipped heartbeat sent a sharp current of alarm through him, and he began to treat his physiology as a potential enemy. His avoidance behaviours settled into routine. He stopped answering the landline after hours, fearing a caller might bring news of another health scare, and he avoided large meals, watching his stomach with steady attention. At work, the constant tension and drifting focus ran alongside his withdrawal. He began excusing himself from afternoon strategy meetings, where the fluorescent lights and overlapping voices coincided with his concentration difficulties. His colleagues noted his quiet distance, and Malcolm accepted it without protest, interpreting the fatigue as proof that he was not yet ready to return to his full responsibilities. Now, at sixty-eight, Malcolm sits in his office chair each morning, the morning briefs stacked beside him, aware of the body on alert and the muscles holding their quiet vigil. His scores on the PCL-5, a solid 77, mirrored the steady intensity of his days. What finally brought him to seek help was not a single crisis, but the quiet accumulation of days where he realized he was living in a state of suspended warning. He does not expect the past to disappear, nor does he fear it will. He hopes, perhaps, to find a way to let his emotions return to their ordinary rhythm, to trust his body again, and to sit through a full meeting without bracing for danger. He is ready to meet his days as they come, with the same careful attention he once brought to policy, no longer certain of what will happen, but prepared to meet it.
